outputs.L1:
Here is a gently polished rendering that preserves every idea and image of the original while smoothing its phrasing:

---

Animula, vagula, blandula.

Life! I know not what thou art,
Yet know that thou and I must part;
And when, or how, or where we met,
I own to me remains a secret yet.

But this I know: when thou art fled,
Where'er they lay these limbs, this head,
No clod so worthless shall there be
As all that then remains of me.

O whither, whither dost thou fly?
Where bend, unseen, thy trackless course?
And in this strange divorce,
Ah, tell me where to seek this compound I?

To the vast ocean of empyreal flame,
From whence thy very essence came,
Dost thou thy homeward flight pursue,
Once freed from matter's base encumbering weed?

Or dost thou, hidden from our sight,
Wait, like some spell-bound knight,
Through blank, oblivious years, th' appointed hour
To break thy trance and reassume thy power?

Yet canst thou, without thought or feeling, be?
O say, what art thou, when no more thou 'rt thee?

Life! we have long been friends together,
Through pleasant and through cloudy weather;
'Tis hard to part when friends are dear—
Perhaps 'twill cost a sigh, a tear.

Then steal away, and give but little warning;
Choose thine own time.
Say not Good night, but, in some brighter clime,
Bid me Good morning.

---

**A note:** These lines are, in fact, the celebrated poem *"Life"* by Anna Laetitia Barbauld, prefaced by the Emperor Hadrian's Latin address to his soul (*"Animula, vagula, blandula"*). Because the piece is already a finished and admired literary work, I have limited myself to light touches of clarity and rhythm rather than substantive rewriting. If you would prefer, I can leave the text entirely in its original, canonical form.
outputs.L2:
Little soul, wandering and gentle. Existence! Your true nature escapes me, yet I understand that a separation between us is inevitable. As for the moment, the manner, or the place of our first encounter—I confess this remains a mystery to me. Still, one thing is certain: once you have departed, no matter where they place these limbs and this head, the dirt of the earth will be no less worthless than whatever is left of me afterward.

Where, oh where, do you soar off to? In what direction does your invisible, untraceable path lead? And in this peculiar separation, please reveal where I ought to search for this blended being that I am. Do you race back toward the immense sea of heavenly fire, the source from which your very substance sprang, once you're released from the lowly, burdensome garment of the body? Or do you, concealed from view, lie waiting—like a knight held under an enchantment—through empty, forgotten centuries until the destined moment arrives to shatter your slumber and take up your strength once more? Can you truly exist devoid of thought or sensation? Tell me, what do you become when you cease to be yourself?

Existence! You and I have journeyed side by side for a long while now, through both fair skies and gloomy ones. Parting is painful when a companion is beloved; it may well bring a sigh or a tear. So slip away quietly, without much warning, and pick your own moment. Do not tell me Goodnight—instead, in some more radiant land, greet me with Good morning.
outputs.L3:
# On the Mystery of Life and Death

The poet stands before one of existence's deepest enigmas: the mystery of life itself. With humble candor, they confess that they cannot truly comprehend its nature—what life fundamentally is, nor how, when, or where they first came to know it. This admission of ignorance is not a failure but a recognition of the profound puzzle that lies at the heart of all conscious being.

Turning to contemplate mortality, the speaker reflects on the striking transformation that death brings. Once life has taken its leave, whatever remains of the body will be rendered as worthless as a common clod of earth. The very vessel that once housed thought, movement, and feeling becomes indistinguishable from the ordinary soil beneath our feet—a sobering reminder of how much life's animating force truly matters.

This reflection naturally gives rise to a searching question: where does the soul, or life-force, go once it departs the body? The poem entertains the possibility that it might return to some vast ocean of celestial flame, rejoining a great cosmic source from which it originally came. Alternatively, perhaps it simply lies dormant, resting in stillness as it awaits some future revival. The mystery admits no certain answer, only wonder.

Pressing further, the poet ponders whether the departed spirit can continue to exist stripped of thought or feeling. If consciousness and emotion are the very qualities that define a soul, what does that spirit become when it is no longer recognizably itself? This question probes the essence of identity and whether anything meaningful can survive its dissolution.

Finally, in a tender and moving turn, the speaker addresses life directly, as one might speak to a long-time companion who has walked beside them through both good times and bad. Rather than resisting the inevitable, the poet asks life to depart gently, without struggle or pain. And in this farewell there is not despair but hope—the promise of a reunion yet to come, in a brighter and more beautiful world beyond.
outputs.L4:
# Life

*A Meditation on Mortality and Hope*

Oh Life, you constant companion through my fleeting years,
What manner of thing are you, that I have never known?
You walk beside me always, yet remain a stranger,
A presence I have felt but never truly seen.

Tell me, dear Life, what is this soul you carry?
This flickering flame of consciousness within?
From whence did it arise, and where, oh where,
Shall it be borne when you at last release your hold?

I have wondered through the long and quiet nights,
When darkness presses close and questions rise unbidden—
What lies beyond the threshold that awaits us all?
Is the spirit merely breath, dispersed upon the wind?

Or does some essence of ourselves endure,
Traveling onward past the final door?
These mysteries have troubled me for years,
And yet no certain answer ever comes.

But now I find my restless spirit calming,
The urgent need to know grows soft and still.
Perhaps not every question needs an answer;
Perhaps in trust alone there can be peace.

So go now, gentle Life, when comes my time—
Depart in quietness, without alarm or grief.
Do not slip away with sorrow's heavy sigh,
Nor let our parting sound like some farewell.

For I have come to see it differently now:
This ending is not truly an ending at all.
When you release me to that greater light,
I will not say "goodbye" to all I've loved.

Instead, I'll greet whatever waits beyond
With hopeful heart and words of glad hello—
Not "farewell" spoken in the fading dark,
But "Good morning" in a bright and dawning realm.

---

*In this poem, the uncertainty that once seemed frightening has been transformed. Death becomes not a closing but an opening, not a final night but the promise of a new and radiant morning.*
outputs.L5:
# Animula

*Animula* — the little soul. It is a word that carries centuries in its small frame, first breathed, perhaps most famously, by the Roman Emperor Hadrian in his farewell verse: *Animula vagula blandula* — "little soul, wandering, gentle." With that single tender word, a dying emperor turned not to conquest or glory, but to the fragile spark that had animated his whole existence.

There is something disarming about naming the soul so small. We tend to imagine life as vast: an accumulation of years, achievements, loves, and losses, spread out like a great landscape behind us. And yet, when we look closely, life reduces itself again and again to something intimate and slight — a breath, a flicker, an *animula* that once wandered gently through the body and now must move on.

Life is the long stretch of experience we cling to. We build homes for it, careers, families, monuments. We fill it with meaning because we cannot bear to think of it as fleeting. And in many ways it is not fleeting at all — a life can be immense, rich, overflowing with significance for those who share it.

*But* — and here is the word that undoes our certainty — everything bends toward its ending. But the body fails. But the years pass more quickly than we thought. But the little soul, so charming and playful, eventually pales, grows cold, and departs to places it cannot describe. That small conjunction, *but*, is the hinge on which all human hope and fear turn. It reminds us that no matter how firmly we hold to life, there is always the qualification, the shadow, the pause before what comes next.

Perhaps this is why Hadrian's words still move us after nearly two thousand years. They do not resolve the tension between life and its ending. They simply hold it — with affection, with uncertainty, with a whispered tenderness toward the *animula* that made everything possible.

We are, each of us, a little soul. We live. *But* we, too, must one day speak our own gentle farewell.

counterfactuals.output:
The poem you're thinking of is traditionally attributed to the Roman Emperor **Hadrian**, said to have been composed as he lay dying. It's addressed not quite to "Life" but to his own **soul** (*animula*), spoken of as the guest and companion of his body. Here is the Latin:

> Animula, vagula, blandula,
> Hospes comesque corporis,
> Quae nunc abibis in loca
> Pallidula, rigida, nudula,
> Nec, ut soles, dabis iocos.

A fairly literal rendering runs something like:

> Little soul, little wanderer, little charmer,
> guest and companion of my body,
> you who now will depart into places
> pale, stiff, and bare—
> and you will not, as you used to, make your jokes.

There are many verse translations. One of the best known in English is by **Lord Byron**:

> Ah! gentle, fleeting, wav'ring sprite,
> Friend and associate of this clay!
> To what unknown region borne,
> Wilt thou now wing thy distant flight?
> No more with wonted humour gay,
> But pallid, cheerless, and forlorn.

Would you like other translations (Pope also made a famous one), or a bit of background on the poem's history?

**To Life, Upon the Soul's Departure**

O Life! thou fleeting, half-remembered guest,
Who lodgest briefly in this mortal breast,
How swift thy hours, how borrow'd all thy breath—
A candle trembling on the sill of Death.

I know thee well: thy joys, thy transient bloom,
Thy laughing mornings hastening to the tomb;
Thy garlands wither ere the day be done,
And every setting mocks the rising sun.

Yet tell me, ere thy latest ember dies,
Whither the spark, the ling'ring vapour flies?
When from these veins the crimson current cease,
And the tired pulse subsides at length to peace—

Does the freed spirit, like a bird unbarr'd,
Ascend beyond the cold and starry guard?
Or, dew-like, melt into the boundless air,
Nor know it was, nor knows that it is there?

I do not dread thee, thou mysterious flight;
The soul that trusts may travel into night.
For He who bade the sparrow fall or fly
Hath surely mark'd the pathway through the sky.

So take thy leave, dear Life; I hold thee fast
No more than mist detains the driving blast.
Yet ere I loose thee, this one grace I crave—
That Hope may light me kindly to the grave.

And when at last the heaving breath be spent,
And this frail frame return to earth, content,
Let not the world lament my quiet room,
But mark how morning conquers every gloom;

For if the soul indeed survive its clay,
'Tis but the dawning of a longer day—
And Life, that seem'd so dear, so brief a span,
Shall prove the shadow, not the whole, of Man.
